news_list.title: India's Industrial Future Depends on the Boring Stuff
news_list.summary:
The future belongs less to countries that pick sectors and more to those that patiently build competence.

Every few months, India falls in love with a new sector.

Semiconductors are the future. Then green hydrogen. Then drones. Then electric vehicles. Policy announcements arrive with billion-dollar incentives; states begin competing for factories, and television debates suddenly discover the word "ecosystem".

But industrial success is not a reality show where governments pick winners and wait for applause. The countries that became manufacturing powers mastered something far less glamorous: capabilities.

That is the real fault line in India's industrial strategy. Delhi still spends too much time choosing sectors and too little time obsessing over the plumbing underneath them: skills, supplier networks, logistics, research capacity, technical education and institutional competence. Factories grab headlines. Capabilities quietly decide whether those factories survive.

To be fair, India today looks far more serious about industrial policy than it did a decade ago. Before 2014, manufacturing policy often drifted between indecision and bureaucratic paralysis. Land acquisition battles dragged endlessly; infrastructure gaps inflated costs, and investors faced regulatory uncertainty severe enough to qualify as a business model. Manufacturing's share in GDP remained stubbornly weak despite India's labour advantage.

The shift since then has been tangible. Highway construction accelerated, digital infrastructure improved dramatically, insolvency reforms strengthened financial discipline, and the Production Linked Incentive scheme pushed manufacturing back into policy focus. Mobile manufacturing became the clearest success story. India, once heavily dependent on imported phones, exported smartphones worth more than $20 billion in 2024-25.

That progress matters. But it also hides a deeper problem.

India still treats industrialisation like an event instead of a process.

A semiconductor plant may generate excitement, but no advanced manufacturing economy is built around isolated factories. It is built around thousands of invisible connections: technicians who can maintain complex machinery, local suppliers capable of precision manufacturing, ports that move components efficiently, universities producing industry-ready engineers, and firms willing to invest in long-term research. Industrial capability is cumulative. Countries build it layer by layer, often over decades.

That insight increasingly dominates modern industrial policy thinking. The debate is no longer whether governments should support industrial development. Most major economies already do. The real question is whether policy is helping firms climb the technological ladder or merely encouraging short-term production targets. Economists studying East Asia repeatedly found that successful industrial economies focused obsessively on learning, capability accumulation and export competitiveness rather than assuming growth would emerge automatically from sector selection.

The difference sounds academic until one looks at how industrial economies actually function.

Taiwan did not become a semiconductor giant because officials woke up one morning and declared chips fashionable. South Korea's manufacturing rise was driven by decades of investments in engineering talent, supplier ecosystems, technical education and globally competitive industrial firms. Industrial strength came from capability accumulation, not policy slogans.

Taking semiconductors again, the government deserves credit for recognising their strategic importance amid growing geopolitical fragmentation. But semiconductor manufacturing is one of the most capability-intensive industries on the planet. It depends on ultra-specialised chemicals, highly trained engineers, precision manufacturing systems, reliable electricity, research partnerships and deeply integrated supply chains. Missing even one layer weakens competitiveness.

The same applies to green manufacturing. India's renewable energy ambitions are substantial and increasingly central to global supply chains. Yet many Indian firms still struggle with technological depth, workforce readiness and research capacity needed for advanced clean-tech manufacturing. Climate ambition without industrial capability risks creating dependence on imported technology rather than reducing it.

This is where India's own economic history offers uncomfortable lessons.

West Bengal was once among India's industrial leaders. Over decades, however, adversarial labour relations, policy rigidity, weakening investor confidence and institutional decline eroded industrial capabilities that had taken generations to build. Once supplier ecosystems collapse and skilled industries migrate elsewhere, recovery becomes painfully difficult. By the time factories stop opening, the deeper damage has usually already happened inside institutions, labour markets and business confidence.

India, today, is clearly in a stronger economic position than it was fifteen years ago. Infrastructure is better, state capacity has improved in several areas, and manufacturing enjoys far greater political attention. But the next phase cannot become a competition to constantly unveil the next fashionable industry while neglecting the foundations that allow industries to endure.

Capabilities scale across sectors. Strong logistics help every exporter. Technical education benefits every advanced industry. Efficient ports, predictable regulation and skilled workers create compounding economic advantages no single subsidy can replicate.

That is the real challenge before India.

Industrial policy works best when governments look beyond the excitement of emerging sectors and focus on building durable national capability.

Because the truth is: factories can be imported. Industrial strength cannot.

news_list.title: Chips still king of Singapore exports amid non-tech upswing in Asia
news_list.summary:
[SINGAPORE] Economists from US investment bank Morgan Stanley, who observed a sharp rise in non-technology exports, recently posed this question: Is Asia's macro story all about semis?

It is undeniable that semiconductors - powerful, ultra-thin wafers - have become a cornerstone of the modern economy.

Growth in the space, which supports the proliferation of artificial intelligence, is powering on in the region, alongside a jump in exports outside the technology sphere, according to the research published on May 20.

The economists noted that non-tech exports from China, India, South Korea and Taiwan - which account for around 60 per cent of Asia's total exports - rose by an annualised 27 per cent in the six months to April 2026.

This mirrored a trend seen across a wider number of Asian economies, where non-tech exports rose by an annualised 25 per cent from October 2025 to March 2026.

Over the period, non-tech exports contributed 8.3 percentage points to overall exports growth, as compared with 3.7 percentage points during the first nine months of 2025.

"While semis exports have continued to accelerate into the second quarter of 2026, non-tech exports are also exhibiting sustained, broad-based strength," the economists wrote.

"The strength of the capex cycle has been key in driving the recovery in non-tech exports," they added. Capex is short for capital expenditure, which refers to the funds that businesses allocate to physical assets like property, technology and equipment.

Singapore, however, has bucked the trend. Electronics shipments, of which chips are a significant driver, have started to account for a bigger share of the Republic's exports.

Year-on-year growth of electronics non-oil domestic exports (NODX) more than doubled from 23.4 per cent in the last quarter of 2025 to 57.8 per cent in 2026's first quarter, thanks to strong artificial intelligence demand.

Chips accounted for S$1.7 billion of the S$3.1 billion in electronics exports in March.

The Republic produces one in 10 chips globally and one in five pieces of semiconductor equipment.

According to the Economic Development Board, the semiconductor industry contributes close to 6 per cent of Singapore's gross domestic product and employs more than 35,000 people.

Meanwhile, non-electronics exports reversed their gains and recorded a year-on-year decline of 3.5 per cent during the first three months of 2026.

DBS senior economist Chua Han Teng told The Straits Times that the weakness "partly reflected headwinds from US tariffs, as non-electronics NODX experienced a significant year-on-year contraction in the first quarter".

He said US President Donald Trump's administration has continued to explore avenues to impose import levies, even after US courts ruled its sweeping reciprocal tariffs and those based on the 1977 International Emergency Economic Powers Act as illegal.

Earlier in June, Trump's trade office in Washington made the first move to replace the sweeping levies with ones he believes are less vulnerable to legal challenges.

Chua also said the results of a US Section 301 investigation into force labour - which, if implemented, will cause a moderate increase in the average effective tariff rate on Singapore - "would likely act as a continued drag on Singapore's non-electronics NODX to the United States".

"Singapore's exporters operating in this space would likely adapt through market diversification efforts, as they brace themselves for continued US trade protectionism, with the US continuing to pursue other investigations under Section 301," he added.

The Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI), in response to the new US tariff proposed on Jun 2, said the 12.5 per cent duty will apply to around one-third of Singapore's domestic exports to the US when it becomes effective.

Some critical exports will remain exempted, including semiconductors and pharmaceuticals and pharmaceutical ingredients.

Elsewhere in Asia, non-tech exports have seen an extended period of growth, driven by ships, networking and telecommunication equipment, and construction machinery, according to Morgan Stanley.

The investment banking firm's economists said: "Part of the strength has come from AI-related products, including power equipment and components."

But they also observed a "momentum in capital goods exports, including industrial equipment and non-passenger car transport equipment".

They added: "Intermediate goods have been the second fastest-growing segment, lifted by the exports of parts which are linked to the production of capital and consumer goods."

Electronics remained a key driver of Singapore's NODX in April, surging 66.7 per cent from a year earlier. Shipments of integrated circuits, or chips, grew by 82.7 per cent.

During the month, non-electronics exports expanded 10.9 per cent, led by pharmaceutical shipments, which soared 97.1 per cent year on year.

UOB associate economist Jester Koh said: "This likely reflects some element of front-loading in response to the US' announced 100 per cent tariffs on selected patented pharmaceuticals and their associated ingredients."

The tariffs are expected to take effect at the end of July for certain large companies, and in September for smaller firms.

An MTI analysis, released earlier in 2026, noted that pharmaceuticals and non-monetary gold had contributed to nominal NODX growth in 2025, but that these exports "tend to be volatile and lumpy".

Koh expects growth in Singapore exports to persist in the months ahead, with the electronics and semiconductor segments continuing to outperform the pack.

"In contrast, non-electronics exports may weaken, reflecting supply shortages in the chemicals segment and a surge in energy prices alongside broader spillovers weighing on external demand," he said.

May's export figures are due to be released next week. THE STRAITS TIMES

items.title: Nissan NV200 Semi Panel Van launched - RM70,900
items.summary:
Edaran Tan Chong Motor Sdn Bhd has just announced a new variant for the Nissan NV200 called the Nissan NV200 Semi Panel Van, which joints its NV200 Panel Van sibling.

The exterior size is about the same, but the Nissan NV200 Semi Panel Van trades some cargo area for a second row of seats just behind the front seats, which can fit up to 3 passengers, turning the NV200 into a 5-seater instead of just a 2-seater. Entry to the rear passenger area is via sliding doors that have fixed glass windows on both sides of the vehicle.

The cargo area now has a volume of 2.33 cubic metros and is accessible through the rear top hinged door. The floor height of the cargo area is 520mm off the ground. There's all full headlining throughout the interior.

The Nissan NV200 Semi Panel Van is powered by a 1.6 litre HR16DE engine with CVTC valve timing, producing 109 PS and 152Nm of torque, mated to a 5-speed manual. The van also has an electric power steering system. Safety features include ABS, EBD, and a single driver airbag.

The Nissan NV200 Semi Panel Van is priced at RM70,900.00 for Peninsular Malaysia and comes with a 3 year or 100,000km warranty. I wonder if ETCM will consider launching a window van (three rows of passenger seats) as well, since now they have a panel and semi panel version. The window van version is called the Nissan Evalia in Indonesia, and is marketed as a competitor to products like the Toyota Avanza or the Daihatsu Luxio. A taxi version of the NV200 with a 2.0 litre engine was picked as the new official taxi of New York City.

topics.topic: 美國股債策略逆勢運作
topics.summary: 根據 MoneyDJ 關於富蘭克林：油價高漲，美國股債策略逆勢運作的報告，美國股債策略逆勢運作成為了一個重要的投資策略。同時，根據 MoneyDJ 的【台股操盤人筆記】在籌碼雜亂中尋找機會的報告，美國股債策略逆勢運作的趨勢正在增強。
根據 MoneyDJ 關於 1.009821 鎖定 AI 原料、能源安全與避險的報告，能源安全與避險成為了一個重要的投資題材。然而，根據【資料庫實體數據證據】，法人資金淨流向為賣超，顯示了法人對這個題材的態度與市場熱度不符，出現了背離的情況。

ai_analysis.full_text:
今日結論：
台股目前是 區間整理 格局，短線以輪動整理為主；現在先看成交、情緒和國際盤能不能一起往同一方向走。

新聞驅動：
今天的題材重點集中在 AI 驅動股市上漲, AI相關題材, 美國股債策略逆勢運作，🇹🇼 MoneyDJ 熱門排行 6 則, 🗞️ 鉅亨網台灣 31 則, 🇺🇸 美股 / 宏觀 8 則。這代表資金正在找主線，市場有反應，但還沒完全定調。

國際與台股：
美股與宏觀訊號以 S&P 500 7394.2998046875 (+1.75%)、Nasdaq 25809.66015625 (+2.54%)、費半 (SOX) 13171.4384765625 (+7.91%)、道瓊 50848.75 (+1.86%) 為主；台股部分，TAIEX 44169.04，漲跌 1019.58，盤面寬度為 808 漲 / 203 跌。夜盤與期貨方面，SGX 資料待補 ，富台 資料待補 。外部訊號仍在對齊中，暫時不算完全同向，但也沒有失控。

KOL與情緒：
台灣市場情緒位於 63（貪婪 (Greed)），CNN F&G 為 29，Crypto F&G 為 12。如果 KOL 方向和盤勢同向，趨勢比較容易延續；如果不同向，代表盤中拉扯還在。

籌碼補充：外資 買超 286.9 億、投信 買超 129.4 億、自營 買超 89.4 億；這組數字可以用來判斷盤勢有沒有延續，而不是只看單日漲跌。
KOL 觀點方面，多方 25%、空方 12%，整體共識度 8 筆；這比較像情緒參考，不是直接的進出場訊號。
操作含意：
綜合來看，等突破再站隊 是比較合理的節奏；如果後續量能和國際盤一起轉強，就順勢跟進；如果情緒先衝太快、指標沒跟上，就先放慢節奏，分批觀察比追價更實際。
